query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a high‐temperature solid lubricant into the CoCrFeNi alloy—specifically by incorporating a moderate weight percent of MoS2—will form a persistent, in situ lubricating film during sliding that lowers friction and wear across the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A monolithic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy produced without any solid lubricant additions, exhibiting higher friction and wear especially at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Introduce 10–15 wt% MoS2 into the CoCrFeNi matrix during processing (e.g., via spark plasma sintering) to create a composite material with uniformly dispersed MoS2 particles.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests under controlled loads in an oxidizing (air) environment, spanning temperatures from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Dispersed MoS2 particles that, upon sliding, generate a continuous and adherent tribofilm at the contact interface.
generation.mechanism: The MoS2 particles provide low shear strength interfaces that reduce tangential forces during sliding. Under both low and high temperatures, these particles (or their decomposed lubricious phases) form a protective film that minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact, thereby reducing friction and abrasive wear, while accommodating elastic–plastic deformation of the matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, the MoS2-modified composite is expected to show a lower coefficient of friction and a reduced wear rate over the entire temperature range (RT to 800 °C).
generation.baseline: Tribological performance (COF and wear rate) of the pure CoCrFeNi alloy under similar sliding, load, temperature, and environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under sliding loads and environmental conditions typical of tribological testing in oxidizing atmospheres. However, its performance may be affected at loads significantly higher than those tested or under non-oxidizing conditions, and the long-term thermal stability of the MoS2 phase at 800 °C remains to be fully determined.
generation.uncertainty: While MoS2 has shown promise in related high-entropy alloy systems, the optimal concentration and its high-temperature stability in a CoCrFeNi matrix are not fully established. There is also some uncertainty about possible oxidation or decomposition pathways of MoS2 at the upper temperature limit that might impair tribofilm formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the pure CoCrFeNi alloy (control) and one modified with 10–15 wt% MoS2 via spark plasma sintering. Subject both sets to identical ball-on-disk sliding wear tests at incremental temperatures (e.g., RT, 400 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C) under consistent loads in an ambient air environment.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) across the temperature range
Surface analysis (SEM, EDS, and XPS) to characterize the presence and continuity of the lubricating tribofilm
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the MoS2-modified samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in both COF and wear rate at all tested temperatures compared to the pure CoCrFeNi control, or if surface analysis fails to show the formation of a continuous or effective lubricating film, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High hardness and good wear resistance have been revealed for the high-entropy alloy (HEA) system AlCoCrFeNiTi, confirming the potential for surface protection applications. Detailed studies to investigate the microstructure and phase formation have been carried out using different production routes. Powder metallurgical technologies allow for much higher flexibility in the customisation of materials compared to casting processes. Particularly, spark plasma sintering (SPS) enables the fast processing of the feedstock, the suppression of grain coarsening and the production of samples with a low porosity. Furthermore, solid lubricants can be incorporated for the improvement of wear resistance and the reduction of the coefficient of friction (COF). This study focuses on the production of AlCoCrFeNiTi composites comprising solid lubricants. Bulk materials with a MoS2 content of up to 15 wt % were produced. The wear resistance and COF were investigated in detail under sliding wear conditions in ball-on-disk tests at room temperature and elevated temperature.
